frames.narration: Ana opens the meeting link. Her app connects a WebSocket to the signaling server and asks to join. The signaling server asks the meeting router where to place her.

The router chooses the Frankfurt SFU, which is 12 ms away. Ana's browser sends an SDP offer and ICE candidates (its own address, one learned from STUN, and a TURN relay) and receives an answer. A direct UDP path to the SFU works, so TURN is not needed.

Ana now sends one encrypted stream of her camera as three simulcast layers: 180p at 150 kbit/s, 360p at 500 kbit/s and 720p at 1,500 kbit/s, 2.15 Mbit/s in all. The media goes straight to the SFU and no longer touches the signaling server.

Ken joins from Tokyo with a weak 4G phone. The router put him on the Tokyo SFU, and the two SFUs are cascaded, so Ana's stream crosses the ocean once, over the backbone, and the Tokyo SFU copies it for the people there.

The Tokyo SFU measures Ken's downlink from packet arrival times: about 1.2 Mbit/s. With 5 tiles on screen it gives the current speaker the 500 kbit/s layer and the other four the 150 kbit/s layer, 1,100 kbit/s in all, which fits with a little room.

Ken starts talking. His audio level, carried in a packet header, is the loudest for a couple of seconds, so the SFUs mark him the dominant speaker. Everyone's app highlights his tile and asks for a higher layer of it.

Recording was started at the beginning. The recorder joined as a hidden participant, subscribed to the tracks and now writes them to storage with timestamps. After the meeting a background job composes one video and a transcript-ready audio file.

Ken walks into a lift and his network collapses. His estimate drops under 100 kbit/s, so the SFU stops his video and keeps the audio, which needs only about 40 kbit/s. Nobody else is slowed. When the signal returns, his layers come back one step at a time.
